question: If a riding group is larger than four or five riders, the manual recommends:
choice_a: Adding a second leader at the back only
choice_b: Dividing it into two or more smaller groups
choice_c: Riding two abreast to shorten the group
choice_d: Keeping it as one large group for visibility
explanation: Small groups make it easier and safer for car drivers who need to get around them. If your group is larger than four or five riders, divide it up into two or more smaller groups.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.33, 'Keep the Group Small'

question: The manual says the group leader should look ahead for changes and signal early so that:
choice_a: Only the second rider needs to react
choice_b: The tailender can pass the leader
choice_c: 'The word gets back' to everyone in plenty of time
choice_d: The group can speed up to close ranks
explanation: Plan -- the leader should look ahead for changes and signal early so 'the word gets back' in plenty of time; start lane changes early to permit everyone to complete the change.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.33, 'Keep the Group Together'

question: Where does the manual recommend placing inexperienced riders in a group?
choice_a: At the very back of the group, out of sight
choice_b: In the middle of the group with no particular placement
choice_c: As the group leader, to build confidence
choice_d: Just behind the leader, so more experienced riders can watch them from the back
explanation: Put Beginners Up Front -- place inexperienced riders just behind the leader. That way the more experienced riders can watch them from the back.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.33, 'Keep the Group Together'

question: If a rider falls behind the group, the manual says the rest of the group should:
choice_a: Slow down a little to stay with the tailender
choice_b: Continue at the same pace and let them catch up on their own
choice_c: Speed up so the group reaches the destination sooner
explanation: Follow Those Behind -- let the tailender set the pace. If a rider falls behind, everyone should slow down a little to stay with the tailender.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.33, 'Keep the Group Together'

question: Why does the manual say everyone in a group should know the planned route?
choice_a: So the group can split up without telling anyone
choice_b: So that if someone is separated, they won't have to hurry to keep from getting lost
choice_c: It is a legal requirement for group rides
choice_d: So only the leader needs a map
explanation: Know the Route -- make sure everyone knows the route. Then, if someone is separated they won't have to hurry to keep from getting lost or taking a wrong turn.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.33, 'Keep the Group Together'

question: In the staggered formation described by the manual, the leader rides in the left side of the lane while the second rider stays:
choice_b: Two seconds behind, in the left side of the lane
choice_c: One second behind, in the right side of the lane
choice_d: Three car lengths behind, in the center of the lane
explanation: The leader rides in the left side of the lane, while the second rider stays one second behind in the right side of the lane.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.33-34, 'Keep the Group Together'

question: In the staggered formation, the third rider maintains the left position and follows the first rider at:
choice_b: No set distance, since spacing only matters for the second rider
explanation: A third rider maintains in the left position, two seconds behind the first rider. The fourth rider would keep a two-second distance behind the second rider.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.34, 'Keep the Group Together'

question: The manual's 'Don't Pair Up' rule means you should never:
choice_a: Operate directly alongside another rider, since there is no place to go if you must avoid a hazard
choice_b: Ride behind another rider at a safe distance
choice_d: Ride with more than one passenger
explanation: Don't Pair Up -- never operate directly alongside another rider. There is no place to go if you have to avoid a car or something on the road. To talk, wait until you are both stopped.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.33, 'Keep Your Distance'

question: The manual explains that keeping close ranks in a group, done properly, has which advantage?
choice_a: It eliminates the need for turn signals
choice_b: It takes up less space on the highway, is easier to see, and is less likely to be separated
choice_c: It allows riders to ignore following distance rules
choice_d: It lets the group ignore posted speed limits
explanation: Maintain close ranks but at the same time keep a safe distance. A close group takes up less space on the highway, is easier to see, and is less likely to be separated -- however, it must be done properly.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.33, 'Keep Your Distance'

question: When passing in a staggered formation, the manual says riders should pass:
choice_a: Two at a time, side by side
choice_b: All at once as a group
choice_d: Only the leader is permitted to pass
explanation: Riders in a staggered formation should pass one at a time.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.34, 'Keep Your Distance'

question: After passing a vehicle, the manual says it is NOT a good idea for the leader to move to the right side of the lane because it:
choice_a: Makes the leader harder for the group to see
choice_d: Encourages the second rider to pass and cut back in before there is enough space cushion
explanation: Some people suggest the leader should move to the right side after passing a vehicle; this is not a good idea because it encourages the second rider to pass and cut back in before there is a large enough space cushion in front of the passed vehicle.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.34, 'Keep Your Distance'

question: The manual says it is best to move into a single-file formation when:
choice_a: Riding curves, turning, or entering or leaving a highway
choice_b: Riding on a long, straight, empty highway
choice_d: Riding at very low speed in a parking lot
explanation: Single-File Formation -- it is best to move into a single-file formation when riding curves, turning, entering, or leaving a highway.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.34, 'Keep Your Distance'
